learningObjectives.text: Explain this episode: Whose situation is central after Troy’s fall?
Use the cited passage to explain: What perspective does the play add to accounts of victory?

main.author: Euripides
main.locator: Trojan Women, Poseidon’s opening speech; Coleridge TEI body, passage on Scamander’s banks and allocation of captives
main.excerpt: desolation seizes on a town, the worship of the gods decays and tends to lose respect. Scamander’s banks re-echo long and loud the screams of captive maids, as they by lot receive their masters. Arcadia takes some, and some the people of Thessaly; others are assigned to Theseus’ sons, the Athenian chiefs.
main.note: Verbatim local text with whitespace normalized. Lesson analysis is interpretation, not part of this quotation.

narrativeBlocks.title: The scene
narrativeBlocks.body: Troy has fallen. Euripides focuses on captive women awaiting allocation to Greek masters, with further losses still ahead. The same war that can furnish heroic fame appears here through enslavement, separation, and mourning.

narrativeBlocks.title: What the source does
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (translation; whitespace normalized): “desolation seizes on a town, the worship of the gods decays and tends to lose respect. Scamander’s banks re-echo long and loud the screams of captive maids, as they by lot receive their masters. Arcadia takes some, and some the people of Thessaly; others are assigned to Theseus’ sons, the Athenian chiefs.”

narrativeBlocks.title: Why it matters
narrativeBlocks.body: Interpretation: Conquest appears as captivity, separation, and inherited trauma rather than as heroic glory.

narrativeBlocks.title: Read it carefully
narrativeBlocks.body: Keep the work’s perspective and authorship visible. Euripides’ tragedy changes whose suffering receives attention; it is not an additional book of Homer or proof of one uniform Greek attitude to war.

narrativeBlocks.title: Carry it forward
narrativeBlocks.body: The chorus turns grief into testimony.

quiz.prompt: What perspective does the play add to accounts of victory?

choices.text: The consequences borne by conquered and enslaved people
An account in which Troy has not yet been attacked
An assurance that captives suffer no further losses
